 Anti-hunger advocates worried about proposed federal SNAP rule that would tighten eligibility
 Maine Public | 
 By
 Patty Wight 
 Published November 13, 2026 at 5:17 PM EST
 Facebook 
 LinkedIn 
 Bluesky 
 Email 
 Allison Dinner 
 / 
 AP file Jaqueline Benitez, who depends on California's SNAP benefits to help pay for food, shops for groceries at a supermarket in Bellflower, Calif., on Feb. 13, 2023. 
 A proposed federal rule that would tighten eligibility for food assistance is facing criticism from anti-hunger advocates in Maine.
 The rule would bar states from automatically qualifying certain people for SNAP benefits if they receive benefits under the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program.
 Robin McCarthy, chief advancement officer for Good Shepherd Food Bank, said the SNAP benefit Mainers receive from automatic eligibility is relatively small, but it makes a big difference.
 "It's like maybe $25 a month for the highest earning salaries on SNAP," McCarthy said. "And when I say highest earning, I think it's important to know that I'm talking about families making between $20,000 to $31,000 a year."
 The Trump administration said the rule would ensure that SNAP benefits are targeted to the neediest households. If approved, the rule would go into effect in 2029. Public comments are being accepted through December 10.
 The proposal comes after federal cuts to SNAP in the 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill." McCarthy said 20,000 Mainers have lost SNAP benefits, including 6,000 children.
